title: Resource Groups: Azure's Unit of Lifecycle
intro: Every Azure resource lives in exactly one resource group. Groups are how you organise, grant access to, and delete things together. Deleting a group deletes everything in it, which is powerful for cleaning up a test environment and catastrophic when aimed at the wrong group.

steps.prompt: List all resource groups in the current subscription as a table.
steps.fake_output:
Name              Location     Status
----------------  -----------  ---------
rg-web-prod       westeurope   Succeeded
rg-data-prod      westeurope   Succeeded
rg-network-hub    westeurope   Succeeded
rg-demo-2023      eastus       Succeeded
NetworkWatcherRG  westeurope   Succeeded
steps.explanation: Five groups, including an old rg-demo-2023 and the NetworkWatcherRG Azure creates automatically.
steps.why: A good naming convention (rg-<app>-<env>) makes the list readable. Groups usually mirror the lifecycle: things that are created and deleted together (one app's environment) share a group.

steps.prompt: List what's inside rg-demo-2023 before deciding anything about it.
steps.fake_output:
Name              ResourceGroup  Location  Type
----------------  -------------  --------  ---------------------------------
vm-demo-01        rg-demo-2023   eastus    Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines
vm-demo-01_OsDisk rg-demo-2023   eastus    Microsoft.Compute/disks
pip-demo-01       rg-demo-2023   eastus    Microsoft.Network/publicIPAddresses
sqldemo2023       rg-demo-2023   eastus    Microsoft.Sql/servers
steps.explanation: An old demo VM, its disk, a public IP, and a SQL server, all still billing.
steps.why: Always look inside before deleting. The SQL server may hold data someone still needs, or it may be the thing a forgotten customer demo still uses.

steps.prompt: Find who owns it: show the tags on rg-demo-2023.
steps.explanation: It was tagged to expire at the end of 2023.
steps.why: Tags like owner and expires turn cleanup from guesswork into policy. Azure Policy can require tags at creation, and a scheduled job can report or delete groups past their 'expires' date.

steps.prompt: Protect the production group rg-web-prod from accidental deletion with a CanNotDelete lock named no-delete.
expected_commands: az lock create --name no-delete --resource-group rg-web-prod --lock-type CanNotDelete
az lock create -n no-delete -g rg-web-prod --lock-type CanNotDelete
steps.explanation: Nothing in rg-web-prod can be deleted until the lock is removed, even by an Owner.
steps.why: Locks guard against the fat-finger scenario (deleting the wrong group) that RBAC can't prevent, because the person who makes the mistake usually has the permission. Removing the lock is a separate, deliberate step.

steps.prompt: After sales-engineering confirms, delete rg-demo-2023 without waiting for it to finish.
steps.fake_output: (no output: deletion started in the background and takes several minutes)
steps.explanation: The group and everything in it is being deleted.
steps.why: --yes skips the confirmation prompt, so only use it after you've checked the name. There's no recycle bin for most resource types. --no-wait returns immediately; check progress with 'az group show'.
